purpose_of_this_fixture: Tests a strong Service discovery call where the client's own word for a ticket tempts a look-alike board, and where three of the things they most want are deferred beyond v1. A facilities maintenance company is missing contractual response times, has been put on a ninety-day performance plan by its largest client, and faces that client's renewal in January. The help desk calls tickets "work orders", so the correct build is the account's NATIVE monday Service Tickets board relabelled to their vocabulary, never a new 'Work Orders' board, and never an extension of the abandoned 'work order tracker' the IT admin built himself two years ago. The client portal they ask for, the email-to-ticket intake they ask for, and per-contract SLA policy calculation are all deferred Service extras: the plugin must say so plainly, design a v1 that works without them (a queue with an owner, a priority in their words and a target date), and put the three on the backlog. The account is loosely described as Standard tier by the IT admin, so plan limits (automation action caps, dashboard board counts, guest and viewer access, single sign-on) and whether Service is provisioned at all are live preflight questions rather than assumptions. Expected verdict: Nearly ready. R2, R3 and R7 are Met and R4 is Partial, because the client gave good hours but explicitly refused to confirm the total until her CFO supplies the real loaded rate. The blueprint, build and first-demo gates are met; pricing and proposal prep stays shut (R4 and R12 Partial, and pricing is out of v1 anyway) even though the client asked for a number to show the CFO. R10 is Partial: a day was agreed but no time, because the CFO's availability is unknown, so the plugin must flag the missing time and propose one. Carries the objection 'monday itself is the problem' (they tried monday two years ago and it did not stick) and 'We'll build it ourselves' from the same IT admin, neither of which appears anywhere else in the fixture set, plus the first existing monday account with live boards belonging to other teams. expected_questions_before_building is the full pool in priority order, not a list to ask in one meeting.
transcript_format: SRT subtitle file. Numbered cues in order from 1, each with a timing line of the form 'HH:MM:SS,mmm --> HH:MM:SS,mmm' (comma before the milliseconds) and cue text that starts with the speaker's display name and a colon: 'Consultant', 'Yvette Carnahan', 'Tansy Whitlock', 'Curtis Vandergrift'. 267 cues running from 00:00:03,000 to 00:41:28,290, so about 41 and a half minutes, with about 5,401 spoken words counted as alphanumeric tokens excluding the speaker labels and timings. Client talk share is 62 percent, just above the method's 60 percent target, and the longest single Consultant cue is 89 words (cue 217), under the 225-word proxy for a long stretch. Three long turns continue into a second or third cue, which repeats the speaker label (cue 175 continues the Consultant's cost arithmetic from cue 174; cues 242 and 243 continue the scope play-back from cue 241), so a quote must sit inside one cue. Deliberate transcript artefacts: cues 13 and 14 are an identical duplicated caption pair ('Tansy Whitlock: Sorry, can you hear me? My headset's being weird.'); cue 33 is mis-attributed, labelled 'Tansy Whitlock' but plainly the Consultant's question ('[laughs] That's a good line. Does anything connect the two?'); '[inaudible]' swallows the name of a competing facilities system at cue 234; '[laughs]' appears several times. No load-bearing evidence sits on the duplicated or mis-attributed cues. Every location in this key is 'cue N, HH:MM:SS,mmm, Speaker Name', taken from the cue the quote sits in, for example 'cue 96, 00:14:05,690, Yvette Carnahan'. The transcript carries no call date and no year.

expected_monday_products.why: IN v1, and the primary build target. The work orders themselves are tickets: they arrive by phone, by a shared email inbox and through two clients' own portals, they carry a contractual response window per client and priority, they get dispatched and escalated, and they have to be reported on monthly per client. All of that belongs on the account's NATIVE Service template boards, above all the native Tickets board relabelled to 'Work Orders' in their own vocabulary, with the board ids detected and recorded at preflight before anything is written. A new 'Work Orders' board, and reviving or duplicating Curtis's abandoned work order tracker, both fail the native-board rule. Three Service extras the client actively wants are deferred beyond v1 and must be named as later work rather than designed: the client-facing portal for Brightmoor's property managers, email-to-ticket intake from the service inbox, and SLA policy setup that works the clock out per contract. v1 carries the window as a priority and a target date on each work order instead, which is what the client said she needs for December.

IN v1, but secondary and to be confirmed rather than assumed. Two candidates the client raised herself and put behind the first cut: preventive maintenance schedules, which are planned recurring visits per contract and are a genuinely different entity from a reactive ticket ('That's a different animal from a call'), currently living in Sage plus Delia's spreadsheet and worth about half the contract value; and the knowledge base that today is a binder plus stale Word documents, which could be monday docs or a board if the account's native Service install has no knowledge-base entity of its own. Both were explicitly 'not first', so they belong on the shown backlog, not in v0.1. No portfolio by default here: the tier is only loosely stated (see expected_structures).

NOT expected, and proposing it would be a mistake. Nobody asked for a pipeline. Ainsworth has client organisations, sites and a renewal at risk, and a plausible-looking CRM story could be spun from the January renewal and the spring county bid, but the client never asked to track either, and the renewal is a retention risk rather than a deal they want managed in monday. Client and site records are needed as linked context for work orders; the honest answer is to ask which existing native board should hold them rather than to create an 'Accounts', 'Clients' or 'Buildings' board. If CRM is ever confirmed, those entities must land on the account's native CRM boards (Leads, Contacts, Accounts, Deals/Opportunities, Activities). monday dev is not indicated at all and is outside v1 in any case.

P1 alone satisfies R2 with a dated incident, a named building, a measured breach (a four-hour window answered in about sixty-six hours) and a workaround the client says fails at exactly the moment it matters. P4 (double entry into the two client portals) is not excavated because its Workaround is Partial, and P5 (knowledge in one person's head) is not, because its Concrete is Partial.

Keep the two dates apart: the next quarterly review is the second week of December, and the renewal decision is January. Neither is stated as a year and the transcript carries no call date.

What is missing is the conversion to money, and she refused to invent it. Freed capacity is named (two people off the portals, and herself out of the escalation path) but never valued. Keeping Brightmoor is the largest upside and she would not size it. Partial, and no figure may be inferred.

Success criteria drafted from these are marked proposed until agreed. The 'ugly and working in December' line is a direct instruction about sequencing, not a throwaway.

The owner. He's not in the weeds on this. He'll ask Pete whether it's a good idea, and Pete will ask me.

If I tell him it's about the January renewal, he'll come.

rubric.note: Met: the tool decision is hers, the spend thresholds are named (over ten thousand the CFO signs, over fifty the owner agrees), the route after a yes is described, what the CFO needs to see is stated, prior budgeting experience is on the record and unflattering (he bought monday two years ago and it was not used, and he has mentioned it since), and she will bring him to the next meeting if it is framed around the January renewal. The approver for spend was not on this call, so the recommendation is to have him in the room next time, which is exactly what the next step is for.

evidence.quote: It's a before-December thing. I want to put something in front of Brightmoor at the December quarterly, even if it's partial. Then January is the renewal decision.
As long as I can see what's late. That's what I need in December.
Whether I can get to December with something that works. If the answer is no, I may as well do the big thing properly next year and take my chances with Brightmoor.

rubric.note: Firmly now rather than later, with a real deadline and an explicit test: something working in front of Brightmoor at the December quarterly review, even if partial. The last quote is also the decision criterion between this and the competing facilities system, so the timeline answer has to be honest rather than optimistic.

evidence.quote: We are missing response times. And it has already cost us.

The inbox. It's a shared mailbox, so everybody can see it and nobody owns it. You open it and there's forty emails, and some of them are work orders and some of them are Marley saying thank you, and you can't tell which ones somebody already dealt with unless they remembered to flag it.

rubric.note: P1 is work orders arriving through three unowned channels and sitting, so contractual response windows are missed and nobody knows until the client says so. Stated plainly by both client-side voices, the director in outcome terms and the help desk lead in mechanism terms.

evidence.quote: The one that hurt was July. Brightmoor, the Carrolton building. A chiller went down on a Friday afternoon. It came into the service inbox at four-something on the Friday and nobody opened that inbox again until Monday morning.

Two floors of offices with no cooling, in July, all weekend. Their property manager called my cell phone on the Monday at seven in the morning. That was a four-hour emergency and we responded in about sixty-six hours.
It's not isolated. It's the weekends and the evenings and the handoffs. Things sit.

rubric.note: A specific dated occurrence with a named client and building, a measured breach against a known window, and a client-side statement that it is a pattern rather than a one-off. The day-to-day shape is also given: evenings, weekends and handoffs.

evidence.quote: We flag them. Or we drag them into a folder. I've got a rule that drops the Fairlane ones into their own folder. And I do a sweep at the end of my day and anything that looks stuck goes on a sticky note on my monitor.
It works when I'm here. It doesn't work when I'm on vacation, it doesn't work at five past five, and it really doesn't work on a Friday at four-something.

rubric.note: The workaround is named in detail (flags, folders, an Outlook rule, an end-of-day sweep, sticky notes) and the client says exactly why carrying on with it is not acceptable: it depends on one person being at her desk, and it fails at the precise moment the July breach happened.

evidence.quote: Me. The supervisors, because I'm the one calling them. And the branch managers when I can't get hold of a supervisor.
And the technicians get it, because they turn up at something that's been sitting three days and the client's already furious with them before they're out of the van.

rubric.note: Reaches the director, the field supervisors, the branch managers, the technicians who absorb the client's anger, and the client's own property managers. Named with how each is affected, not just who.

evidence.quote: Reactive, so calls, four hundred-ish a week across the three branches. More in the summer when the air conditioning starts going.
That was a four-hour emergency and we responded in about sixty-six hours.
And we have already lost a client over it. Not Brightmoor. Cavender Medical, back in March. Six clinics.

rubric.note: Met on the method's terms, which accept frequency and errors as cost inputs: a weekly volume, a measured breach, and a lost client. No money is attached to P1 itself. The volume is hedged ('four hundred-ish') and explicitly excludes preventive maintenance, and the lost client was never valued, so neither belongs in a bleed figure. Partial is a defensible reading for anyone who requires a money input.

evidence.quote: In a year? If we lose Brightmoor in January then we're not growing, we're shrinking, and I'd be looking hard at whether I need nine people in client services. rubric.note: A direct answer to the trajectory question with two mechanisms: losing the largest client shrinks the business and the team, and the work they are bidding for carries more reporting obligation than the work they have. Internal only, since it includes possible headcount reduction.

evidence.quote: I build it. Every month. I pull the spreadsheet, filter it to that client, and go line by line working out whether we made the window.
Because I can't take it into a quarterly review if I don't believe it. And last time I didn't believe it, and I was right not to.

rubric.note: P2 is the monthly per-client service level report being rebuilt by hand from the spreadsheet, and not being defensible when it matters.

evidence.quote: We had ninety-four percent on our sheet and they had seventy-eight on theirs. And I couldn't defend either number in the room. That's worse than being wrong. I sat there with nothing to say.

The date it came in and the date the technician closed it. Except the date it was closed is the date I typed it in, which might be two days after he actually did it. So I know it's not right. I have to go and ask people.

rubric.note: A specific occurrence with both numbers, plus the root cause in the client's own words: the recorded closure date is when the help desk typed it in, not when the technician did the work. That single fact is a hard data-quality requirement for the build.

evidence.quote: Two days. Give or take. Two days out of my month. And then Yvette reads it and finds something that doesn't look right and I do parts of it again.
So I know it's not right. I have to go and ask people.

rubric.note: The workaround is manual reconstruction plus asking people, and why it fails is stated: the result still cannot be believed, so it gets partly redone, and it still could not be defended in the room.

evidence.quote: Delia pulls the PM completion part out of Sage, because that's in the report too. That's another half day of hers.
Half a day a month, more with the follow-up. I'm not going to put a number on my own time.

rubric.note: Three people touch the monthly cycle (the help desk lead, the director, and Delia for the preventive maintenance completion part out of Sage), and the client's own credibility in front of the client is the fourth casualty.

evidence.quote: Two days. Give or take. Two days out of my month. And then Yvette reads it and finds something that doesn't look right and I do parts of it again.
Call it twenty. My two days isn't always two days.
Delia pulls the PM completion part out of Sage, because that's in the report too. That's another half day of hers.

rubric.note: Hours are given per person and then revised down by the client herself: the components sum to about twenty-four hours a month, and she said 'Call it twenty'. Use twenty, her figure, and record twenty-four as the arithmetic alternative; the method says never round up. No money is attached, because the director refused to price her own time, so these hours stay hours.

evidence.quote: I mean, it just, it's the same every month. It's not getting worse exactly. It's just always there.

rubric.note: Partial: she answered the trajectory question but with a flat, vague answer. It is a standing monthly cost rather than a worsening one, and no growth or volume effect is described. Do not convert 'always there' into a trend, and do not treat the absence of worsening as a reason to drop the pain: the reporting is what the December quarterly review turns on.

evidence.quote: There isn't one, really. There's me calling Dewey.
Officially, if a work order is going to blow its window, or the technician can't get in, or it needs a part we haven't got, we escalate it to the field supervisor for that trade in that region.

evidence.quote: Every day there's one or two. Out of, I don't know, fifteen or twenty escalations a day across the branches, a couple of them just vanish, and then somebody remembers at four o'clock.

rubric.note: Day-to-day shape with what, how often and the consequence: one or two of fifteen to twenty daily escalations vanish and resurface late in the afternoon. Both figures are hedged and are volumes to confirm, not cost inputs.

evidence.quote: I keep a list on a legal pad and I re-text people. That's the system. It's a legal pad.
Call or text. Usually text.

rubric.note: Named, and the client's own judgement on it is in the repetition: the system is a legal pad. Why it falls short is explicit elsewhere in the same exchange (a client is on hold while nobody knows whether the supervisor has the message).

evidence.quote: The client feels it first. Then me, because they ring me. And the supervisors will tell you they're getting texted about the same job by three different people, which is also true.

rubric.note: Reaches the client first, then the director, then the supervisors who are texted about the same job by several people. The last part is a requirement in disguise: one visible escalation record per work order rather than several parallel texts.

evidence.quote: An hour a day each, easily, for the people who aren't stuck on the portals. Just chasing and re-asking.
Seven, with me.

rubric.note: An hour a day each for seven people, which is the thirty-five hours a week half of the sixty-five-hour figure. The client qualified it as 'easily', so it is a floor rather than a midpoint, and the rate that would turn it into money is the CFO's to supply.
Not discussed. Nothing was said about what happens to escalation volume as the business grows or if nothing changes, and the question was not asked. It becomes a gap question for the scoping call.

evidence.quote: Brightmoor and Fairlane. Everything they send us we have to accept in their system, then when it's done we close it in their system with a note, and photos sometimes. And we still have to have it in our spreadsheet, because the dispatcher hasn't got a ServiceChannel login.
Twice, or three times. And their system logs you out every twenty minutes.

traps: The vocabulary trap at the centre of this fixture: 'work order' is this client's word for a ticket, and 'request' is the same thing by their own account. The build must relabel the account's NATIVE Service Tickets board to 'Work Orders', not create a board of that name. A hand-built 'Work Orders' board with the right columns still fails the rule.

Curtis's abandoned monday 'work order tracker' from two years ago is the second half of the same trap. It is still in the account and full of dead work orders. Reviving it, duplicating it, or building the new queue beside it all fail: the ticket entity belongs on the native Service board, and the old board is something to audit, archive or leave alone by agreement.

'PM' means preventive maintenance, never project manager. PMs are contracted recurring visits planned months ahead, they live in Sage plus Delia's spreadsheet, they are about half the contract value, and the client called them 'a different animal from a call'. They are a separate entity from reactive tickets and were explicitly put behind the first cut.

'Portal' means two different things in this call. The client-owned vendor portals (ServiceChannel for Brightmoor, Fairlane's own system) are where work is re-keyed today. The client-facing portal Yvette wants is a deferred Service extra. Do not conflate them, and do not promise either.

All three of the extras this client wants most are deferred beyond v1: the customer portal, email-to-ticket from the service inbox, and SLA policy setup that calculates the clock per contract. The plugin must name all three as later work, put them on the backlog, and still deliver a v1 that helps, which is a queue with an owner, a priority in their words and a target date.

The client pushed back directly on the email-to-ticket deferral, because the July breach was an email nobody opened. The answer has to be honest: on day one a person still opens the inbox, and what changes is that the work order then sits in a visible queue with a clock. Promising automatic email intake in v1 to win the point is the failure mode here.

Their priority language is three words and nothing more: emergency, urgent and routine, each tied to a contractual window. They never use numbered priority codes on this call, so do not invent a 'P1, P2, P3' coding scheme for the priority column or the status labels; use their words. Separately, the method's own pain ids P1 to P5 are internal and must never appear in anything client-facing, which is a different rule about a different set of labels.

The account tier is loose and unverified: 'Standard, I think? Whatever the middle one is. I'd have to look.' Plan limits that actually bear on this build (monthly automation action caps, how many boards a dashboard can combine, guest and viewer access, single sign-on, and which columns are available) must be read live at preflight, never assumed from that line.

Microsoft single sign-on is a stated IT requirement that may not exist on their current plan. Raise it as a plan question with a cost implication; do not promise it, and do not quietly design around it either.

Whether monday Service is provisioned at all is unknown. The only known monday use is Work Management boards belonging to other teams. If Service is not provisioned there is no native Tickets board to build on, and the correct behaviour is to stop and ask, never to hand-build a look-alike in Work Management.

This is the first fixture with a live monday account holding other teams' work: a safety inspections board and an estimating bid board, fifteen to twenty users, and an unknown administrator. Audit it, leave those boards alone, and settle which workspace the build belongs in before writing anything.

'We tried monday two years ago and it didn't stick' is the platform objection, and the transcript supplies its own answer: nothing arrived in the old board automatically, so it was double entry against the spreadsheet the dispatcher actually used, and nobody asked the help desk before it was built. Establish whether the setup or the tool was the cause before entertaining any switch, and do not repeat the same design.
Do not add the unquantified items to any cost figure: the Cavender Medical loss is 'six clinics' with no value, the Brightmoor contract value was declined twice, and the July breach was never priced.
'Just under a fifth of our book' is a proportion with no revenue base. It cannot be turned into a dollar figure, and the base must not be inferred from headcount or industry averages.

The $35 loaded hourly cost is the director's own guess, offered with 'Don't hold me to that' and then explicitly withdrawn pending the CFO. The Consultant's roughly $118,300 a year is arithmetic on an unconfirmed rate, not a bleed. R4 stays Partial and pricing prep stays held.

expected_structures.notes: Service is the engagement and the native-board rule governs it. Preflight must confirm Service is provisioned, detect the native Tickets board and any companions actually needed, record their ids per entity in the client record, and record the change check, all before a single write. The three Service extras stay out of v1 and on a visible backlog: no customer portal object, no email-to-ticket channel, and no SLA policy setup, which means that where the native Tickets board already carries SLA helper columns they are left alone and no response-time promises enter the blueprint. Do not add native companions nobody asked for (satisfaction surveys, asset registers) just because the family ships them. The Work Management side (preventive maintenance schedules, possibly the knowledge base) is ordinary built structure, is not governed by the native-board rule, and was explicitly deferred behind the first cut, so it belongs on the backlog rather than in v0.1. Four client-stated constraints must survive into whatever shape is built: a client has many buildings and a work order belongs to a building; the closure timestamp must reflect the work, not the data entry, or the monthly report inherits today's flaw; the escalation view has to work on a phone; and opening a work order must not mean re-typing client, building and contact. The two client-owned portals stay manual in v1 because closing work there is a payment condition and the API route is unconfirmed in someone else's tenant. Sage 300 remains the system of record for money and PM schedules. Automations go to the Consultant as one list for a single approval, with recipients named per row, the action cap on the real plan checked against four hundred-plus work orders a week, and a turn-off step per automation in the handoff because API-created automations cannot be switched off through the API.

Equally acceptable: stopping short of a build because preflight shows Service is not provisioned, and asking. What fails is a hand-built look-alike board of any name, and reusing the abandoned work order tracker.

Naming the customer portal, email-to-ticket and SLA policy setup as deferred beyond v1, putting them on a visible backlog, and still designing a v1 that addresses the July breach through a visible queue with an owner, a priority in their words and a target date. Promising any of the three in v1 to satisfy the client's push-back is the failure.

Either sequencing of the first build passes: the whole four-part first cut, or the queue and the report first with escalation second pending the supervisor conversation. What fails is designing escalation as a desk workflow, or designing it at all without talking to a field supervisor as the client asked.

Treating the platform objection as a current-state finding: asking what monday failed to do, establishing that the old attempt died of double entry and of nobody consulting the help desk, and saying plainly that the same design would fail again. Arguing for the platform, or going quiet on it, both fail.

Answering the build-it-ourselves question the way the method suggests, by asking what held it up last time and whose week it would come out of, and proposing that the admin keeps the parts only he can do. Dismissing his competence, or agreeing to a handover that makes every change a ticket to him, both fail.

Grading R10 Partial and flagging that no time was agreed, with a recap that proposes specific times. Grading it Met because a day and an owner exist is tolerable only if the missing time is still flagged and proposed.

Grading P5 Concrete Partial rather than Met, and P5 Reach, Cost inputs and Trajectory Missing rather than inferring them from the four-month ramp or from her wish to take a vacation. Marking Cost inputs Partial on the strength of the four months is a tolerable alternative that changes nothing.

Reading the account live at preflight rather than trusting 'Standard, I think': the plan, seats, administrator, whether Service is provisioned, the automation action cap against four hundred-plus work orders a week, dashboard board limits, guest access for subcontractors, and whether single sign-on exists on that plan or needs a plan change the CFO must approve.

Auditing the existing account, leaving the safety and estimating boards untouched, proposing what to do with the dead work order tracker rather than silently reusing it, and asking whether the build belongs in that workspace or a new one.

Not proposing a portfolio, and recording why (tier loosely Standard and unverified; Work Management secondary and deferred; the work is a queue, not projects). Revisiting it only if preflight finds Enterprise and the preventive maintenance side is agreed as Work Management.
Not proposing CRM, and not reading the January renewal or the spring county bid as a pipeline. Asking which existing native board should hold client, site and contact records is the right move.

Presenting the automations as one list for a single approval, each row naming trigger, conditions, action and exact recipients, with the note that API-created automations cannot be switched off through the API and a turn-off step per automation in the handoff.

Using their vocabulary throughout (work order, request, PM, emergency, urgent, routine, the clock, building, supervisor, the quarterly) while keeping the method's own vocabulary, pain ids, grades and cost figures out of anything client-facing. Their priorities are labelled in their three words, never with invented codes such as P1 to P3; those are the method's internal pain ids and belong nowhere near client-facing material.
